headline: First Nation Leads Kelp Forest Restoration in British Columbia
meta_description: A partnership between the Tla-o-qui-aht First Nation and restoration groups is replanting kelp forests in Clayoquot Sound, drawing on indigenous knowledge.
summary_short: Indigenous-led initiative in Clayoquot Sound grows and transplants young kelp to restore degraded forests and rebuild coastal ecosystems.
body:
In Clayoquot Sound on Canada's Pacific coast, the Tla-o-qui-aht First Nation is partnering with the Redd Fish Restoration Society and West Coast Kelp to revive kelp forests that have degraded over time. Launched in early 2026, the project operates a nursery where bull kelp and giant kelp grow safely away from sea urchins and other grazers before being harvested and replanted. So far, the team has restored 4,200 square meters—roughly the size of ten basketball courts—but the work signals a larger possibility: that kelp forests can be brought back more effectively when restoration is guided by both science and ancestral wisdom.

The initiative does more than replant seaweed. It merges indigenous knowledge with modern restoration practice. Tatt Charlie, a tribal guardian of the Tla-o-qui-aht, explains that his ancestors operated on a principle of reciprocity, taking only what was needed and always giving back. That philosophy now shapes where and how the project plants kelp, with the goal of returning the territory to its state from 300 years ago. Emily Fulton, the marine program manager for the Redd Fish Restoration Society, emphasizes that the real work ahead involves measuring impact—understanding exactly how restored kelp forests benefit the wider ecosystem and the species that depend on them.

What makes this effort noteworthy is not just its ecological ambition, but its foundation. By centering Tla-o-qui-aht leadership and oral history in the restoration process, the project treats kelp restoration as an act of cultural recovery as much as environmental repair. The nursery is still small, a beginning. Yet it demonstrates how traditional knowledge and contemporary conservation can work together to heal coastal waters.
quick_facts: Partnership launched early 2026 in Clayoquot Sound, British Columbia
Tla-o-qui-aht First Nation leads effort with two restoration partners
4,200 square meters replanted so far—about ten basketball courts
Nursery grows bull kelp and giant kelp away from grazing sea urchins
Project guided by 300-year-old indigenous principles of reciprocity
